## CS-31 — Setting Up Your Computer


**Do this before the Week 1 lab.** If you're having trouble, we'll help you during the Week 1 lab session. If you get stuck, post on Piazza or come to office hours — do not spend three hours fighting it alone.

**Time:** about 20 minutes, most of it waiting for downloads.
**Disk space:** you need about 2 GB free. The course environment itself is roughly 1.3 GB.
**You do not need administrator rights** on your machine.

---

## What you are installing, and why

Four separate things work together. It helps to know which is which when something breaks.

| Thing | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Python** | The program that actually runs your code. |
| **uv** | A tool that installs Python for you and manages the exact set of libraries this course needs. |
| **VS Code** | The editor where you open and run notebooks. |
| **The course folder** | A folder containing the labs *and* a recipe listing every library, so everyone in the class runs identical software. |

You will not install Python yourself. `uv` does that in Step 3.

---

## Step 1 — Install uv

Pick your operating system.

### macOS

Open **Terminal** (press ⌘+Space, type "Terminal", press Enter) and paste:

```
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

### Windows

Open **PowerShell** (press the Windows key, type "PowerShell", press Enter) and paste:

```
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
```

The `-ExecutionPolicy ByPass` part is required — Windows blocks scripts downloaded from the internet unless you say otherwise. If your machine is managed by an employer or refuses the command, use this instead:

```
winget install --id astral-sh.uv --exact
```

**Then run this second command as well:**

```
winget install --id Microsoft.VCRedist.2015+.x64
```

This installs a Microsoft system library that the optimization solver we use in Week 4 depends on. Many Windows machines already have it, in which case the command will simply tell you so and exit — running it costs you nothing. Without it, Week 4's solver will crash your notebook with no useful error message.

### Linux

```
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

If you are using **WSL on Windows**, run the *Linux* command inside your WSL shell, not the PowerShell one. WSL has its own filesystem and its own PATH; the Windows copy of uv will not be visible from inside it.

---

## Step 2 — Close your terminal and open a new one

**This step is not optional.** The installer added uv to your PATH — the list of places your computer looks for programs — but that change only reaches terminal windows opened afterwards.

Close the window. Open a fresh one.

**Check it worked:**

```
uv --version
```

You should see something like `uv 0.12.5`. If you see "command not found" or "not recognized", see Troubleshooting below.

---

## Step 3 — Get the course folder and build the environment

Download the course folder from Canvas and unzip it.

**Where you put it matters.** Put it somewhere with a short, simple path and **not** inside a cloud-synced folder:

| | Good | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | `/Users/yourname/cs31_env` | anything inside iCloud Drive |
| Windows | `C:\Users\yourname\cs31_env` | Desktop or Documents if OneDrive is syncing them |
| Linux | `~/cs31_env` | — |

Cloud sync tools try to upload the thousands of small files the environment creates. This is slow, and it can corrupt the environment while it is being built.

Now, in your terminal:

```
cd ~/cs31_env
uv sync --compile-bytecode
```

On Windows use `cd C:\Users\yourname\cs31_env`.

This one command does four things: it reads which Python version the course uses, downloads that Python if you do not have it, creates a private folder called `.venv` inside the course folder, and installs every library at exactly the version the rest of the class is using.

Expect this to take several minutes the first time. It downloads about 1 GB.

**Check it worked:**

```
uv run python -c "import ortools, pgmpy, mesa; print('ok')"
```

You should see `ok`.

---

## Step 4 — Install VS Code

Download from <https://code.visualstudio.com> and install.

- **Windows:** choose the **User Installer**, not the System Installer. The User Installer does not need administrator rights.
- **macOS:** drag the app into your Applications folder.
- **Linux:** use the `.deb` / `.rpm` for your distribution, or your package manager.

---

## Step 5 — Open the course folder in VS Code

In VS Code: **File → Open Folder** and choose your `cs31_env` folder.

VS Code will show a notification in the bottom-right offering to install the recommended extensions. **Click Install.** This installs the Python and Jupyter extensions, which are what let you run notebooks.

If you miss the notification, open the Extensions panel (the four-squares icon on the left) and install:

- **Python** (by Microsoft)
- **Jupyter** (by Microsoft)

---

## Step 6 — Confirm VS Code found the right Python

Look at the **bottom-right corner** of the VS Code window. It should mention `.venv`.

If it does not, or if you are unsure:

1. Press **Ctrl+Shift+P** (Windows/Linux) or **⌘+Shift+P** (macOS) to open the Command Palette.
2. Type `Python: Select Interpreter` and press Enter.
3. Choose the `cs31_env` entry that has `.venv` in its path — it should be listed as "Recommended".

---

## Step 7 — Run the environment check

Open `labs/setup_test/check_env.ipynb` from the file list on the left.

At the **top right** of the notebook, click where it says **Select Kernel**, choose **Python Environments**, and pick the `.venv` entry.

Then click **Run All**.

If the last cell prints a success message, you are done. Screenshot it or note the versions — if something breaks later in the semester, this is the baseline.

## Working day to day

**Starting a lab.** Open VS Code, **File → Open Folder → cs31_env**. Add the folder for this weeks lab into the **cs31_env** folder. Open the notebook, run cells. That is all. You should not need to type anything in a terminal.

**Running Python from the terminal**, if you ever want to:

```
cd ~/cs31_env
uv run python my_script.py
```

The `uv run` prefix means you never have to "activate" anything — uv figures out which environment to use from the folder you are in.

**When the course environment changes.** Occasionally a new library gets added for an upcoming lab. You will get an announcement. Download the updated course folder (or `git pull` if you are using git), then run:

```
uv sync --compile-bytecode
```

This adds what is new and changes nothing else. It is safe to run any time.

**Installing something for your own project.** Do not add it to the course folder. Make a separate folder for your project:

```
uv init ~/cs31-project
cd ~/cs31-project
uv add pandas scikit-learn
```

## Troubleshooting

### `uv: command not found` / `'uv' is not recognized`

You did not open a new terminal after installing (Step 2). Close every terminal window and open a fresh one.

If that does not fix it on **Windows**, the installer put `uv.exe` in `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin`. Confirm it is there, then restart your computer.

### The install command is blocked or fails on Windows

Your machine may be restricting scripts. Use `winget install --id astral-sh.uv --exact` instead.

### `uv sync` fails partway through

Usually the network. Run it again — it resumes rather than starting over.

If it fails repeatedly on campus wifi, try a different network. If it complains about disk space, you need about 2 GB free.

### VS Code says "no module named ortools" but `uv run` works fine

VS Code is using the wrong Python. Go back to Step 6 and select the `.venv` interpreter explicitly.

If selecting `.venv/bin/python` (or `.venv\Scripts\python.exe`) does not stick, try again and choose **Enter interpreter path**, then paste the path to the **`.venv` folder itself** rather than to the python file inside it.

### The notebook has no kernel, or the kernel keeps dying

Click **Select Kernel** at the top right, choose **Python Environments**, pick `.venv`. If it still dies, close VS Code entirely and reopen the folder.

### I already have Anaconda / Miniconda installed

That is fine, but it will clutter the interpreter list. Pick the entry containing `cs31_env/.venv` and ignore the conda ones. Do not run `conda activate` while working on this course.

### The kernel crashed / died, and it happened at an OR-Tools cell (Windows)

**Symptom:** "The Kernel crashed while executing code in the current cell", often with exit code `3221225477`. No Python error, just a dead kernel.

**Cause:** Windows is missing a Microsoft C++ system library that OR-Tools needs. This is not something you did wrong, and everything else in the notebook can work fine while this fails.

**Fix:** In PowerShell:

```
winget install --id Microsoft.VCRedist.2015+.x64
```

Then close VS Code entirely, reopen it, and run the notebook again from the top.

### A yellow `SyntaxWarning` about escape sequences appeared when importing axelrod

Harmless, and it only appears once. Python prints it the first time it compiles that library and never again afterwards. If you followed Step 4 exactly (`uv sync --compile-bytecode`) you should not see it at all.

### Everything is broken and I want to start over

Delete the `.venv` folder inside `cs31_env` and run `uv sync --compile-bytecode` again. This is safe — your notebooks are not inside `.venv`.

Stop and post in the course Piazza with:

1. Your operating system and version
2. The exact command you ran
3. The full error message (please copy the text, not screenshot it)
